narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 69.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Being in the bottom decile, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students, signaled to the model that you may struggle with the demands of the bar exam. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and similarly pulled the prediction toward failure; again you placed in the lowest decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential feature, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.00 it is only modestly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so the model saw this as a mild positive signal that slightly reduced the estimated risk of failure.

Taken together, the two very low class rankings outweighed the decent GPA and raised the predicted failure risk high enough to deny admission. Gender, race, family income bracket, LSAT score, and full-time status played no role in this outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in law school so that your class rank improves significantly. Stronger upper-year grades are the clearest way to shift future predictions in your favor.
